cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights because the trial court never prescribed written norms of parental conduct the father was expected to meet, and it announced prospectively that a termination-seeking party must prove parental potential for harm by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: Judicial clarity in the prescribed norms of parental conduct is essential to the preservation of the procedural safeguards mandated by state and federal due process.

relevance.ACT-01: Sets the constitutional floor for any correction-of-conditions plan: services a parent is asked to accept voluntarily must be translated into conduct norms clear enough to be complied with.
relevance.ACT-02: This is the leading Oklahoma authority requiring the court itself to prescribe clear, written norms of parental conduct before a service-plan failure can be used against the parent.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding and deprived adjudication alone do not give a parent notice of what must change; C.G. requires judicially specified conduct norms before that finding can support later action.
relevance.OUT-02: C.G. is the source of Oklahoma's clear-and-convincing standard for termination and of the pre-termination notice requirement that governs every TPR appeal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held that a parent whose child has been adjudicated deprived is entitled to a jury trial in a State-initiated proceeding to terminate parental rights under Okla. Const. art. 2, § 19, overruling contrary prior decisions.
cases.quote: We find that parental rights are too precious to be terminated without the full panoply of protections afforded by the Oklahoma Constitution.

relevance.DEC-05: Filing a deprived petition that contemplates termination triggers the jury-trial right A.E. recognized, which shapes how the case must be pleaded and tried from the outset.
relevance.OUT-02: A.E. is the foundational Oklahoma holding that a parent facing State-sought termination has a constitutional right to trial by jury.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Guardianship of M.R.S.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of a never-unfit natural father's application to end a non-relative guardianship, holding the post-decree change-of-custody test does not apply and that custody may be withheld from a parent only on clear and convincing proof of unfitness.
cases.quote: for custody to be taken from the parent there must be a showing, by clear and convincing evidence, of unfitness of the parent

relevance.INP-05: When a parent voluntarily hands care to a guardian rather than to the agency, M.R.S. governs the terms on which the parent can get the child back.
relevance.DEC-06: M.R.S. explains why a non-court, non-petition arrangement cannot silently harden into a permanent loss of custody absent proof of unfitness.
relevance.OUT-03: M.R.S. is the controlling Oklahoma statement of the burden and presumption that apply when guardianship is used as a permanency arrangement.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a psychologist who reported suspected child abuse, holding the statutory good-faith reporting privilege bars every theory of recovery for harm flowing from the report unless the plaintiff pierces it with proof of bad faith.
cases.quote: The broad statutory privilege extends across all cognizable theories of liability.

relevance.INP-01: Myers is the controlling Oklahoma authority on the scope of the mandatory reporter's statutory immunity and on what a plaintiff must show to overcome it.
relevance.INP-02: The same privilege protects any person who reports in good faith, not only listed professionals, which is what makes voluntary third-party reporting practicable.
relevance.INP-04: The report here arose out of a contested custody matter, and Myers holds that the litigation context does not itself supply bad faith.
relevance.INP-06: Good faith is presumed by statute, so an anonymous or low-detail report does not strip the reporter of immunity absent proof of guilty knowledge.
relevance.INP-07: Myers arose from a clinician's report about her own patients' disclosures and is the leading Oklahoma case on health-professional reporting exposure.
relevance.DEC-02: Because immunity attaches to the report and to participation in the resulting proceedings, it also covers allowing agency access to the child during investigation.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of a maternal grandmother's guardianship, holding the mother had not carried her burden of showing both that the impediment to her custody was gone and that ending the guardianship would not be inimical to the child's welfare.
cases.quote: When the impediment to the natural parent's custody has been removed, the guardianship is no longer necessary unless its termination would be inimical to the welfare of the child.

relevance.INP-05: Ovalle is the Oklahoma template for the parent-initiated placement with kin and for what the parent must later prove to undo it.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows the limits of resolving a safety problem outside a deprived petition: the private arrangement is durable and not unwound on request alone.
relevance.OUT-03: Ovalle supplies the two-part test that decides whether a kinship guardianship stays in place as the child's permanency outcome.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed orders continuing visitation with a reunification goal and directing a change of foster placement, finding no abuse of discretion in the trial court's weighing of conflicting evidence about the child's best interests.
cases.quote: In making such decisions, the paramount consideration remains the best interests of the child.

relevance.ACT-03: B.T.W. confirms that a court may order DHS to move a child out of a foster home whose environment does not promote the permanency plan.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's statement of how a reunification-directed visitation plan is reviewed when foster caregivers resist it.
relevance.OUT-04: The case illustrates the court's continuing supervisory power over placement and visitation while the youth remains in agency custody.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reinstated a jury verdict terminating a mother's parental rights, holding that clear and convincing evidence showed she failed to correct the substance-abuse conditions and that termination served the child's best interests.
cases.quote: In parental termination cases, the State must show by clear and convincing evidence that the child's best interest is served by the termination of parental rights.

relevance.INP-03: The case began with a joint DHS and police entry into a suspected drug house, the classic law-enforcement referral pathway into an Oklahoma deprived case.
relevance.INP-07: Positive drug testing of the parent was the evidentiary engine of the case, illustrating how medical and toxicology findings feed the child-welfare record.
relevance.INP-10: It shows an intake contact escalating within a week into a filed deprived petition on the same facts.
relevance.DEC-03: Daniels states the standard of proof and the appellate canvass that a substantiated-conditions theory must ultimately satisfy.
relevance.ACT-02: The disposition order's list of court-ordered conditions is the operative service plan that the termination case was later measured against.
relevance.ACT-05: Domestic-violence counseling was a court-ordered condition, showing how protective measures short of removal are folded into the plan.
relevance.OUT-02: Daniels is the modern Oklahoma Supreme Court restatement of the clear-and-convincing best-interests standard for termination.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of H.M.W. (West v. State)
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held that although an imprisoned father's failure to appear triggered 10A O.S. § 1-4-905(A)(5), he remained entitled under that statute to a jury trial in absentia, so terminating his parental rights without a jury was error.
cases.quote: Upon review, we find that § 1-4-905(A)(5) does apply, but conclude that Mr. West was entitled to a jury trial in absentia as provided in this statute.

relevance.INP-11: The children were Cherokee Nation eligible and the case was governed by both the federal and Oklahoma Indian Child Welfare Acts, with the Nation participating throughout.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held the Governor holds a constitutionally grounded deliberative-process privilege that can withhold records from an Open Records Act request, but that the privilege is qualified and enforceable only through in camera judicial review with the burden on the executive.
cases.quote: This privilege is not absolute, however, and is subject to the check and balance of in camera judicial review, in lieu of legislatively-mandated public disclosure.

relevance.INP-09: Oversight bodies seeking executive-branch child-welfare deliberations will meet this privilege and must invoke in camera review.
relevance.FAIL-06: Vandelay defines the outer limit of an Oklahoma agency's ability to refuse disclosure and the judicial remedy when it does.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit requests touching executive deliberations are resolved under the in camera balancing this case prescribes.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels seeking policy-level documents face this privilege and the burden allocation announced here.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the leading recent Oklahoma transparency decision and the practical ceiling on state-level public-records claims.
relevance.PMC-06: Systemic analysis of state decision-making must account for the withholding power recognized, and limited, in this opinion.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Department of Human Services v. Jones (In re T.T.S.)
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: Resolving a split among Court of Civil Appeals panels, the court reversed a termination judgment and held that due process requires the particular conditions a parent failed to correct be specified in the State's application, the jury instructions, the verdict forms and the final order.
cases.quote: Given the gravity of the rights implicated, vigilant enforcement of the full panoply of procedural safeguards must be carried out in child deprivation cases.

relevance.INP-04: The opinion directs trial courts to secure an incarcerated parent's participation and proper service, shaping how court-driven case activity must be conducted.
relevance.ACT-02: T.T.S. holds that a sprawling ISP mixing mandatory and merely desired items does not adequately identify the conditions a parent must correct.
relevance.OUT-01: Because reunification turns on which conditions must be corrected, the specificity rule here defines what the parent must actually accomplish.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the current Oklahoma Supreme Court template for reversing a termination on fundamental instructional and procedural error.
relevance.PMC-01: Systemic instruction and pleading defects of the kind corrected here are exactly the judicial-determination quality issues federal reviews examine.
relevance.PMC-06: The opinion documents an acknowledged, court-recognized systemic inconsistency across appellate divisions, a concrete weak point for structural analysis.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held that the cognitive-disorder ground in 10A O.S. § 1-4-904(B)(13) is not the exclusive basis for terminating the rights of a parent with a diagnosed disorder, and affirmed termination under the general failure-to-correct ground where the mother had notice, services and well over three months to comply.
cases.quote: These provisions are not mutually exclusive, but complement one another.

relevance.ACT-02: B.K. holds that a mental-health treatment requirement can be an ISP condition the parent must correct, not merely a diagnosis-based ground.
relevance.ACT-06: The case turns on a parent's refusal of psychiatric medication and the State's ability to make accepting treatment a condition of reunification.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's most direct treatment of disability-based termination grounds and the due-process protections that accompany them.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of M.A.S.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed an order declaring a child eligible for adoption without the biological father's consent because the record lacked clear and convincing evidence that his partial nonpayment of support was willful or that he had the ability to pay in full.
cases.quote: unless the trial court's determination rests on clear and convincing evidence, that determination will be reversed

relevance.OUT-02: M.A.S. is the current Oklahoma Supreme Court statement of the proof required to sever a parent's consent right and clear the path to a stepparent adoption.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding DHS made reasonable reunification efforts despite the absence of visitation the children refused, that clear and convincing evidence supported the jury's verdict, and that trial counsel was effective.
cases.quote: We find the district court did not abuse its discretion when it found that DHS made reasonable efforts toward reunification.

relevance.ACT-01: The opinion catalogues the counseling and other voluntary services DHS supplied and treats their provision as the measure of adequate front-end effort.
relevance.ACT-02: In re C.M. holds that completing the ISP alone does not entitle a parent to custody, which defines the practical weight of a court-ordered plan.
relevance.DEC-06: The court emphasizes the Children's Code purpose of preventing removal and preserving family ties where safety permits.
relevance.OUT-01: This is the leading recent Oklahoma reasonable-efforts decision and the benchmark for when a reunification plan may be abandoned.
relevance.FAIL-03: The court applies the seventeen-month reunification-services ceiling and the fifteen-of-twenty-two-month filing duty that implement federal ASFA and Title IV-E requirements.
relevance.PMC-01: Reasonable-efforts judicial determinations of this kind are the precise data point federal Child and Family Services Reviews score.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of S.A.H.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the grandparents' adoption and the dismissal of a cousin's competing guardianship claim, holding the cousin had no statutory or constitutional right to custody of, or to notice of the adoption of, the child.
cases.quote: Cousin had no right--by statute or constitution--to notice of Grandparents' adoption.

relevance.INP-05: A relative's self-initiated request to take a child does not, by itself, create standing or a right to be heard in a competing permanency proceeding.
relevance.ACT-04: S.A.H. marks the boundary of kinship preference: extended relatives beyond those the statutes name have no entitlement to placement or notice.
relevance.OUT-03: It holds that an adoption decree extinguishes a pending guardianship claim by a relative, which determines how kinship permanency competitions end.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of K.G. v. Department of Human Services
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of foster grandparents' objection to DHS's emergency removal of their foster child, holding that the reasonable-suspicion standard governs whether an emergency justified physically removing a child from a foster home.
cases.quote: the trial court is faced with an inquiry into whether an emergency exists to justify physical removal of the child from an existing foster home, the reasonable suspicion standard applies

relevance.INP-12: The opinion adopts a lesser, reasonable-suspicion showing for emergency action precisely because a prompt hearing follows.
relevance.DEC-04: K.G. distinguishes the emergency decision to remove from the later decision where to place, applying different standards to each.
relevance.ACT-03: It is the leading Oklahoma decision on a foster parent's right to object to removal and the standard the agency must satisfy.
relevance.ACT-04: The foster parents were the child's grandparents, and the case shows kinship status does not raise the agency's burden to move the child.
relevance.OUT-04: It defines the court's role in policing placement stability for a child who remains in long-term agency custody.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination judgment and remanded for new trial, holding that a parent's stipulation entered at the preponderance-level adjudication stage cannot be given preclusive effect on the elements the State must later prove by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: we view the recited stipulation as reflecting only Mother's concession that State could prove the allegations of the deprived petition by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.DEC-03: Gordon holds that an agency-substantiated, parent-stipulated adjudication is not an admission that survives into the higher-burden termination phase.
relevance.DEC-05: It warns that the way a petition is resolved by stipulation controls how much the State must still prove later.
relevance.OUT-05: The decision returns the case for retrial rather than closure, illustrating how a defective adjudication record unwinds downstream outcomes.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed a deprived adjudication that rested on a DHS worker's recounting of the child's and other declarants' out-of-court statements, because the trial court made none of the reliability and trustworthiness findings the hearsay statutes require.
cases.quote: Subsection B(l) imposes upon the trial court an affirmative duty to make a specific finding of reliability, according to a general set of criteria.

relevance.INP-08: The case turns on how a child's disclosure, elicited in an investigative interview, may be relayed into court, the same problem that arises with school disclosures.
relevance.INP-10: It exposes the record gap that results when the circumstances prompting DHS involvement and the initial interview are never documented.
relevance.DEC-02: Frazier is the key Oklahoma authority on the evidentiary limits of investigative child interviews, including recorded forensic interviews.
relevance.DEC-03: Substantiation resting on unexamined hearsay cannot support an adjudication without the statutory reliability determination.
relevance.DEC-05: The opinion shows what the State must be prepared to prove admissibly once it files a deprived petition.
relevance.OUT-05: The judgment was reversed and remanded for new trial even though custody with DHS was left undisturbed.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a clean example of appellate reversal of an agency-driven adjudication for procedural and evidentiary error.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights because the record contained no clear and convincing evidence supporting the statutory grounds alleged against him.
cases.quote: We hold that the record does not include clear and convincing evidence supporting termination in this case and reverse.

relevance.OUT-02: Khan is the Oklahoma authority for the proposition that incarceration alone, without record proof of the statutory elements, cannot terminate parental rights.
relevance.OUT-05: The reversal ends the State's termination case against this parent for want of proof.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a direct example of appellate reversal of a termination for evidentiary insufficiency against an absent, incarcerated parent.

cases.case_name: Cherokee Nation v. L.S. (In re B.B.A.)
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed a decree of adoption of an Indian child by a non-Indian family, finding no abuse of discretion in the trial court's conclusion that the biological parents' unified placement preference in a voluntary proceeding was good cause to deviate from the ICWA and OICWA preferences.
cases.quote: We cannot find the district court abused its discretion when it determined good cause existed to deviate from the statutory adoptive order of preferences

relevance.ACT-04: The case marks the principal Oklahoma exception to mandatory tribal and extended-family placement preference in voluntary placements.
relevance.FAIL-05: It addresses head-on when deviating from a race- and tribe-conscious statutory preference is lawful rather than discriminatory.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed an order transferring a deprived proceeding to tribal court as to one child, holding ICWA § 1911(b) gives either parent an unconditional veto over transfer and that the objecting father need not show good cause for his objection.
cases.quote: The trial court erred in directing the transfer of the case as to S.F. over Wood's objection.

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling Oklahoma decision on parental objection to transfer of jurisdiction to a tribal court under ICWA § 1911(b).

cases.case_name: Katherine E. v. State, Department of Human Services
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the dismissal of out-of-state grandparents' adoption petition, holding they had standing after the parents' rights were terminated and that DHS's statutory power to consent to an adoption does not displace the court's duty to hear them on the child's best interests.
cases.quote: the trial court erred when it dismissed Grandparents' adoption petition based on the best interests of the child, without providing Grandparents an opportunity to be heard

relevance.ACT-04: It establishes that DHS's placement and consent preferences cannot foreclose a relative's statutory and due-process right to be heard.
relevance.OUT-03: Katherine E. defines grandparents' standing to seek kinship permanency once parental rights have been terminated.
relevance.FAIL-01: The decision is a direct reversal of an agency-driven dismissal that denied relatives notice and a hearing.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed a deprived adjudication, holding the State could re-remove and refile after the first case failed for want of a petition within seven days, that holding the emergency custody hearing on the third judicial day violated the two-day rule but did not divest jurisdiction or deny due process, and that competent evidence supported the adjudication.
cases.quote: The burden of proof is on the State to demonstrate the factual basis for the deprived status adjudication by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.INP-03: The removal followed a law-enforcement-referred abuse suspicion and shows the affidavit-and-order mechanics Oklahoma uses at that stage.
relevance.INP-04: The case maps the sequence of court orders, from ex parte emergency custody order through show-cause hearing, that judicial actors control.
relevance.INP-10: It traces the escalation from an initial abuse suspicion to a second emergency custody order and a filed petition.
relevance.INP-12: Gurley is the leading Oklahoma case on the two-judicial-day emergency custody hearing deadline and the consequences of missing it.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds an emergency removal may be repeated on the same facts after a procedural dismissal, a significant limit on parents' remedies.
relevance.DEC-05: The seven-day petition deadline and its enforcement are the subject of the first half of the opinion.
relevance.OUT-05: The first deprived case was dismissed and the child returned solely because the State missed the filing deadline.
relevance.FAIL-02: Gurley is the Oklahoma decision squarely holding that a statutory timing violation in emergency custody does not itself make the ensuing custody unlawful.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court remanded a termination appeal for an evidentiary hearing on the mother's claim that trial counsel failed to interview or subpoena witnesses, adopting a record-supplementation procedure for ineffective-assistance claims in parental-rights cases.
cases.quote: This general rule limiting the right to counsel (and to effective counsel) to criminal cases, however, does not control in termination of parental rights cases.

relevance.FAIL-01: Burrell is the Oklahoma procedural vehicle for attacking a termination judgment on the ground that appointed counsel was constitutionally ineffective.

cases.case_name: Porter v. Comstock ex rel. Department of Human Services
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the award of adoption to the children's out-of-state first cousin over long-term tribal foster parents, holding the foster parents had not shown good cause by clear and convincing evidence to depart from ICWA's extended-family placement preference.
cases.quote: the Porters did not demonstrate good cause, by clear and convincing evidence, to deviate from the mandatory placement preferences of the ICWA

relevance.ACT-04: Porter holds that ICWA's extended-family preference outranks both attachment to a long-term foster home and the state kinship-preference statute.
relevance.FAIL-05: It confirms that preferring a non-tribal relative over a tribal foster home is required by ICWA's family-first ordering, not a discriminatory choice.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held that placing Indian children with their mothers after emergency removal from the father was a foster care placement triggering ICWA § 1912(d), and affirmed the finding that the State made active efforts by clear and convincing evidence before adjudication.
cases.quote: We find no reason why the same case-by-case review should not be applied when deciding if State has made the required active efforts in this foster care placement.

relevance.INP-11: The opinion construes ICWA's definitions to reach placements with a non-custodial parent, expanding when tribal protections attach.
relevance.ACT-03: It defines when an out-of-home arrangement counts as a foster care placement for federal purposes even though the child lives with a parent.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failing to apply § 1912(d) to a parent placement is the kind of ICWA compliance gap this decision corrects.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a new trial, holding ICWA's active-efforts requirement did not apply because no existing Indian family relationship would be broken up, and alternatively that clear and convincing evidence showed active efforts were made and had failed.
cases.quote: we conclude § 1912(d) of ICWA is inapplicable because there was no relationship or Indian family entity to breakup

relevance.ACT-01: Simmers marks the outer limit of the duty to offer remedial and rehabilitative services to a tribal-member parent who never had a relationship with the child.
relevance.FAIL-03: It applies Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl in Oklahoma and defines when an active-efforts omission is not a compliance failure at all.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: In an action arising from the murder of a child DHS had placed with her biological father, the court affirmed that the Governmental Tort Claims Act's child-placement exemption bars tort claims against DHS, but reversed and remanded for trial on a state constitutional due-process claim that DHS employees acted in reckless disregard of a known risk.
cases.quote: the Legislature, under 155(29), has exempted DHS from tort liability under the GTCA

relevance.INP-09: The case is the clearest Oklahoma appellate record of what an after-the-fact review of a fatal placement decision looks like.
relevance.DEC-01: It shows the consequences when DHS possesses risk information and does not act on it before finalizing a placement.
relevance.OUT-04: The decision defines the residual remedies available to a child who is harmed while the agency retains responsibility for her placement.
relevance.OUT-06: Deal is the leading Oklahoma authority on civil liability following a child fatality connected to an agency placement decision.
relevance.FAIL-04: It holds that GTCA immunity does not extinguish a state constitutional claim where DHS employees recklessly disregarded a known or obvious risk of serious harm.
relevance.PMC-01: Fatal-placement litigation of this kind surfaces the safety-outcome failures federal reviews are meant to detect.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion documents how statutory immunity insulates the agency from the ordinary financial accountability of tort liability.
relevance.PMC-03: It illustrates why external citizen review matters where the tort system is closed off by legislative exemption.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of the Cherokee Nation's motion to transfer a guardianship of an Indian child to tribal court and ordered the transfer, because the guardians opposing transfer did not carry their clear-and-convincing burden of proving good cause to keep the case in state court.
cases.quote: We conclude the Guardians did not provide clear and convincing evidence of good cause for the trial court to decline Cherokee Nation's request to transfer jurisdiction to tribal court.

relevance.INP-11: C.H.S. is the current Oklahoma statement of the burden and standard governing tribal transfer motions, including in guardianship cases.
relevance.OUT-03: It holds that a guardianship of an Indian child is subject to ICWA transfer even after the guardianship has been in place for years.

cases.case_name: West v. Jane Phillips Memorial Medical Center
cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed statutory reporting immunity for all harm flowing from a hospital's mandated report of a false-positive drug screen after childbirth, but reversed as to claims for harm unconnected to the report, such as negligent pre-testing protocols and alleged harassment.
cases.quote: The grant of summary judgment in Defendants' favor for harm not connected with the report to DHS was in error and is REVERSED.

relevance.INP-01: It draws the operative line for mandatory reporters: immunity covers post-reporting harm only, not independently negligent conduct that produced the underlying information.
relevance.INP-07: The case is the leading Oklahoma decision on hospital drug screening of new mothers and the reporting duty that follows a positive result.
relevance.FAIL-06: The plaintiff's breach-of-confidentiality theory shows how disclosure of medical information in the reporting chain is litigated in Oklahoma.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the boundary between protected mandated disclosure and actionable mishandling of personal health information.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court vacated a deprived adjudication as to a father because the trial court treated the mother's no-contest stipulation as binding on him and denied the non-jury trial he requested, and remanded for a trial meeting ICWA standards.
cases.quote: We therefore find that the trial court committed reversible error in denying Father's request for a non-jury trial

relevance.INP-11: On remand the adjudication must satisfy ICWA's clear-and-convincing, qualified-expert-witness standard for foster care placement of an Indian child.
relevance.DEC-05: The case holds that one parent's stipulation to the petition cannot adjudicate the other parent's child deprived.
relevance.OUT-05: The adjudication as to the father was vacated outright, returning his part of the case to square one.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a direct appellate reversal of an agency-and-court shortcut that bypassed a non-offending parent's right to a hearing.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed adjudication and immediate termination of a mother's parental rights for failure to protect her children from the father's sexual abuse, holding that trying the case two years past the statutory adjudication deadline neither destroyed jurisdiction nor denied due process.
cases.quote: the court did maintain jurisdiction of the matter and the delay in the adjudication hearing did not violate mother's constitutional guarantee of due process of law

relevance.DEC-05: The opinion addresses a petition that sought adjudication and immediate termination together, and the timing rules that then apply.
relevance.ACT-05: The mother's agreement to withdraw a protective order and permit unsupervised visitation was the core of the failure-to-protect finding.
relevance.ACT-06: The court relies on 10A O.S. § 1-4-207, which lets a court immediately assume custody and order medical or behavioral health treatment to protect a child.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed a jury verdict terminating a mother's rights to six children, holding DHS's services were adequate despite her claim that trauma-informed care was withheld, and that the heightened ICWA proof requirements were met as to the Indian children.
cases.quote: we find DHS' attempts to help Mother in her efforts to reunite with the children were more than adequate

relevance.ACT-05: The case measures the sufficiency of protective and therapeutic interventions offered to a parent with a severe trauma history.
relevance.OUT-01: It sets the Oklahoma benchmark for when a parent's complaint that services were not individualized enough will fail to defeat termination.

cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a counselor who reported that her own patient posed a threat of sexual abuse to his daughter, holding negligence or even gross negligence in making the report does not pierce the statutory good-faith immunity, which also covers reports of threatened rather than completed abuse.
cases.quote: Although Dr. Kishur's affidavit may support a finding of negligence or even gross negligence, we conclude it fails to provide support for a finding of bad faith.

relevance.INP-01: Kremeier is the Oklahoma decision holding that 10A O.S. § 1-2-104 immunity covers reports of predicted or threatened abuse, not only abuse already occurring.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms the presumption of good faith and the plaintiff's heavy burden to rebut it in any suit against a reporter.
relevance.INP-06: The decision shows that a low-certainty, speculative report is still immunized absent guilty knowledge or an evil mind.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit held that caseworkers who entered a family's home and removed a child without a warrant, prior notice or a hearing, in the absence of exigent or extraordinary circumstances, violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, though the defendants might still establish qualified immunity on remand.
cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances.

relevance.INP-08: Roska supplies the Tenth Circuit's baseline rule that child-welfare investigation is not a "special needs" exception to the warrant requirement.
relevance.INP-12: It is binding circuit law on what protective custody without judicial authorization requires in Oklahoma.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision governs how far investigators may go physically into a home before a warrant becomes necessary.
relevance.DEC-04: Roska is the controlling Tenth Circuit authority that removal without prior notice and hearing requires extraordinary circumstances.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement into foster care that begins with an unconstitutional entry and seizure is itself constitutionally infirm.
relevance.ACT-06: The removal was justified below by concerns about the child's medical treatment at home, and the court rejected that as a special need dispensing with a warrant.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the leading § 1983 wrongful-removal precedent binding on Oklahoma federal courts.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit adopted the majority rule that state officials may remove a child without prior notice and hearing only when they have a reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the child's safety, judged on all relevant circumstances including whether judicial authorization could have been obtained, and must provide a prompt post-removal hearing.
cases.quote: even in these instances in which emergency removal is justified, the state must afford the parents a prompt post-removal hearing

relevance.INP-12: Gomes fixes the substantive standard and the post-removal hearing duty that govern Oklahoma protective custody as a matter of federal due process.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Tenth Circuit's definitive articulation of the exigency test for removing a child before a court order issues.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal that fails the reasonable-suspicion test, or that is not followed by a prompt hearing, is actionable under § 1983 in this circuit.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to a caseworker who recommended placing and keeping a child in his father's custody and failed to investigate mounting evidence that the father was abusing him, holding this violated clearly established state-created-danger law.
cases.quote: Ms. Patton's conduct violated T.D.'s clearly established substantive due process right under Currier to be free from state-created danger.

relevance.DEC-01: Screening out or closing on known abuse indicators can itself be the constitutional violation where the agency has already placed the child.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement recommendations are affirmative acts for which a caseworker can be personally liable when they create or increase danger to the child.
relevance.OUT-06: The case sets the Tenth Circuit framework for serious-injury claims arising out of an agency-directed placement.
relevance.FAIL-02: It establishes caseworker personal liability in Oklahoma's circuit for placement decisions made in conscious disregard of known abuse evidence.
relevance.FAIL-04: T.D. v. Patton is the controlling danger-creation precedent for harm suffered by a child under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion documents in detail the investigative failures a fatality or near-fatality review is designed to surface.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: In a suit arising from Oklahoma DHS's seizure and questioning of a child at school, the Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the DHS specialist and the sheriff's deputy on the Fourth Amendment claim, reversed as to the officer who merely transported the child, and reversed on the familial-association claim as not clearly established.
cases.quote: Unless officials have judicial authorization, however, they cannot seize a child without at least having reasonable suspicion of imminent danger.

relevance.INP-03: The seizure was executed jointly by a DHS worker and law enforcement, and the court parses each actor's independent duty to assess suspicion.
relevance.INP-06: The court holds that an anonymous hotline call, without corroboration or indicia of reliability, does not supply reasonable suspicion.
relevance.INP-08: Halley is the governing Tenth Circuit case on seizing and interviewing a child at school without parental consent or a warrant.
relevance.INP-12: It is Oklahoma-arising circuit authority on the minimum showing required before a child may be taken into protective custody.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision constrains how an accepted report may be investigated through custodial questioning of the child.
relevance.FAIL-02: Halley confirms that an Oklahoma DHS worker who seizes a child without reasonable suspicion of imminent danger is not entitled to qualified immunity.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance standard for permanent neglect proceedings violates the Due Process Clause, and that before a State may irrevocably sever the rights of parents in their natural child it must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: Santosky explains why an agency finding made on a lesser standard cannot by itself carry the weight of a permanent severance decision.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal constitutional floor for every termination of parental rights, including those litigated under Oklahoma's Children's Code.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a state child-protection agency that knew of and investigated abuse but left the child in his father's home did not violate the Due Process Clause, because the Clause imposes no affirmative duty to protect a person from private violence absent a custodial relationship.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.DEC-01: DeShaney is the reason a screen-out or unfounded closure, standing alone, rarely produces federal liability no matter how foreseeable the later harm.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the starting point for any claim arising from a fatality or serious injury to a child the agency knew about but did not remove.
relevance.FAIL-04: DeShaney and its custody and danger-creation exceptions define the entire federal liability landscape for harm to a supervised child.
relevance.PMC-04: Because federal damages liability is largely foreclosed, fatality review and legislative oversight carry the accountability function in this area.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that "domicile" in the Indian Child Welfare Act has a uniform federal meaning, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents are domiciled on the reservation, and that exclusive tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) therefore applied notwithstanding the parents' voluntary off-reservation surrender.
cases.quote: Tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) was not meant to be defeated by the actions of individual members of the tribe

relevance.INP-11: Holyfield is the controlling federal decision on when ICWA strips a state court of jurisdiction altogether, a live question in Oklahoma given its many tribes.
relevance.FAIL-03: A state court that proceeds where exclusive tribal jurisdiction exists has entered a void order, the most serious form of ICWA non-compliance.
relevance.FAIL-05: The opinion grounds ICWA's tribal preferences in tribal sovereignty and the tribe's own interest in its children, not in racial classification.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed both termination orders, holding the second was void because entered while the first was on appeal and the first violated due process because the indigent mother was never advised that counsel would be appointed for her.
cases.quote: The fundamental nature of parental rights requires that the full panoply of procedural safeguards must be applied to child deprivation hearings.

relevance.FAIL-01: Chad S. is the foundational Oklahoma due-process authority in child deprivation cases and the original source of the 'full panoply of procedural safeguards' language later quoted in T.T.S.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court granted a writ prohibiting enforcement of an adoption decree obtained ex parte by one grandparent, holding that grandparents whose custodial claims stand co-equal with the petitioner's were affected or interested parties constitutionally entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard.
cases.quote: Our view is, and we hold, that by the inexorable command of both the state and federal fundamental law notice to these petitioners was indeed their constitutional due.

relevance.ACT-04: Muggenborg is the Oklahoma Supreme Court source of the rule that relatives with a co-equal custodial claim cannot be cut out of a placement decision without notice, the authority Katherine E. applies.
relevance.OUT-03: It establishes that once the parental bond is gone a grandparent has standing to claim custody and must be heard before kinship permanency is awarded to someone else.

cases.case_name: Michael F. v. State ex rel. Department of Human Services (In the Matter of D.D.F.)
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of an adoptive father's parental rights but held, as a question of first impression, that because counsel must be provided in Oklahoma termination proceedings, that right necessarily includes effective assistance measured against an objective standard of reasonableness.
cases.quote: The right to counsel would be of no consequence if such counsel were not required to represent the parent in a manner consistent with an objective standard of reasonableness.

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Oklahoma Supreme Court holding that the right to counsel in a termination case includes effective assistance, the premise on which Burrell later built its record-supplementation procedure.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of R.W.S.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a non-relative couple's adoption petition, holding that where a court order deferred the father's child support there was no clear and convincing evidence of a willful failure to support that would make the child eligible for adoption without his consent.
cases.quote: The standard of proof in determining a child's eligibility for adoption without parental consent is clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: R.W.S. is part of the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court line fixing the clear-and-convincing burden and the willfulness element before a father's consent right can be severed for nonsupport.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of A.M. and R.W.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed a jury termination verdict, reviewing the procedural due process claim de novo and holding that a parent may be excluded from the courtroom during a child's testimony only on a showing at a hearing of significant emotional harm, but that this mother showed no impairment of her defense.
cases.quote: a parent should not be excluded from the courtroom absent a showing at a hearing that the child would suffer significant emotional harm caused by the parent's presence

relevance.OUT-02: A.M. and R.W. supplies the Oklahoma Supreme Court's de novo standard of review for procedural due process challenges to a termination trial and the limits on excluding a parent from the child's testimony.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of Baby Boy L.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed an order declaring an Indian child eligible for adoption without the father's consent, abandoning the judicially created existing Indian family exception in light of amendments to the Oklahoma ICWA and expressly overruling In re S.C., Baby Boy D and D.M.J.
cases.quote: the "existing Indian family exception" is no longer a viable doctrine applicable in Oklahoma insofar as Indian child custody proceedings are concerned

relevance.ACT-01: Baby Boy L. removes the escape hatch a state agency could otherwise use to avoid ICWA's remedial and rehabilitative service obligations toward a tribal-member parent.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling Oklahoma authority that a state court may not decline to apply ICWA on the theory that no Indian family existed, the compliance failure Simmers flirts with.
relevance.FAIL-05: The opinion rejects an exception whose practical effect was to withhold ICWA's protections from parents based on how Indian a court judged their family to be.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court vacated the Court of Civil Appeals opinion and affirmed the deprived adjudication of all four children, holding a therapist's account of a child's statements was admissible under the medical diagnosis or treatment hearsay exception and that competent evidence supported the adjudications.
cases.quote: On appeal from an order declaring a child deprived, we will affirm the trial court's findings if they are supported by competent evidence.

relevance.DEC-02: J.D.H. defines when statements a child makes during treatment following an investigation may be repeated in court, the counterpart to Frazier's limits on investigative interviews.
relevance.DEC-05: It is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's statement of the preponderance burden and competent-evidence review that govern a filed deprived petition through adjudication.
relevance.INP-10: The case arose from the family's fourth DHS referral in six months, showing how repeat intakes escalate into emergency custody and a filed petition.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: In the second B.T.W. appeal the court affirmed a post-appeal permanency order that kept the child with her foster mother, limited the mother to supervised visitation and changed the permanency plan to long-term out-of-home placement, finding reasonable efforts had been made and no abuse of discretion or due process violation.
cases.quote: A trial court's findings concerning visitation and placement of a child previously adjudicated as deprived are matters of equitable cognizance.

relevance.OUT-01: This is the later B.T.W. decision that supplies the abuse-of-discretion standard for reviewing a reasonable-efforts finding, the standard In re C.M. applies.
relevance.ACT-03: It confirms the trial court's continuing equitable power over where a deprived child is placed and how much contact the parent gets.
relevance.OUT-04: The case is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's approval of long-term out-of-home placement as a permanency plan when reunification is no longer realistic.

cases.case_name: Oklahoma Public Employees Ass'n v. State ex rel. Oklahoma Office of Personnel Management
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court held that the Open Records Act's personal-privacy exemption lists examples non-exclusively and requires a case-by-case balancing of privacy against the public's interest in knowing how government operates, and that under that test state employees' birth dates and identification numbers may be withheld.
cases.quote: when the balancing test is applied to the facts presented, release of birth dates and employee identification numbers of State employees "would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy"

relevance.FAIL-06: OPEA fixes the Oklahoma test a requester must satisfy when an agency refuses disclosure on personal-privacy grounds, the most common refusal in child-welfare records practice.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and spending records requests are resolved under the balancing framework this case adopts for the Open Records Act.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels seeking agency records about identified individuals will meet the privacy exemption construed here.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's leading construction of the Open Records Act privacy exemption and its federal FOIA analogue.

cases.case_name: Bosh v. Cherokee County Building Authority
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: Answering certified questions, the court held that Okla. Const. art. 2, section 30 supplies a private damages action for excessive force notwithstanding the Governmental Tort Claims Act, that the action applies retrospectively to cases then in the pipeline, and that respondeat superior governs municipal liability for it.
cases.quote: The Okla. Const. art 2, § 30 provides a private cause of action for excessive force, notwithstanding the limitations of the Oklahoma Governmental Tort Claims Act

relevance.FAIL-04: Bosh is the trunk of the state constitutional damages theory that Deal v. Brooks grafted onto child-welfare facts, and no Deal argument is complete without it.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the origin of the only Oklahoma damages route around governmental immunity for a child seriously harmed or killed in state custody or state-directed placement.
relevance.PMC-02: The decision is the Oklahoma Supreme Court's statement of when statutory immunity stops shielding an agency from financial accountability.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an unwed father's parental rights, holding he was denied due process because he was never given adequate notice of the pregnancy and birth and there was no clear and convincing evidence supporting termination under the adoption statute.
cases.quote: Father had a right, under the Due Process Clause, to notice of the fact that Mother was pregnant with his child.

relevance.OUT-02: K.P.M.A. is the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court authority on the notice a biological father is constitutionally owed before his consent right can be severed to clear an adoption.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: The court affirmed the transfer of a deprived case to Cherokee Nation tribal court, holding ICWA became applicable prospectively when the mother enrolled and that the State and foster mother failed to prove good cause by clear and convincing evidence to keep the case in state court.
cases.quote: When ruling on a motion to transfer jurisdiction to tribal court, the party opposing transfer has to prove good cause to keep the case in state court by clear-and-convincing evidence.

relevance.INP-11: M.H.C. is the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court authority on ICWA transfer motions, including when ICWA attaches mid-case, and is the decision C.H.S. applies.

cases.case_name: Barrios v. Haskell County Public Facilities Authority
cases.court: Supreme Court of Oklahoma
cases.holding: Answering certified questions, the court declined to extend Bosh and held that because the Legislature amended the Governmental Tort Claims Act in 2014 to define constitutional violations as torts subject to the Act, article II sections 7 and 9 do not allow an inmate to sue the State for denial of medical care.
cases.quote: these "constitutional" torts are now clearly "torts" governed by the GTCA

relevance.FAIL-04: Barrios is the Supreme Court's narrowing of Bosh and is essential to any honest assessment of whether Deal v. Brooks's state constitutional route to liability survives the 2014 GTCA amendments.
relevance.OUT-06: It shows the Legislature's power to close the damages remedy for harm suffered in state custody, the same power that produced the child-placement exemption in Deal.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion documents how legislative amendment can eliminate the financial accountability a court had recognized only five years earlier.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an evidentiary hearing is not required before termination of Social Security disability benefits, and announced that what process is due is determined by weighing the private interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation and the value of added safeguards, and the Government's interest including fiscal and administrative burdens.
cases.quote: identification of the specific dictates of due process generally requires consideration of three distinct factors

relevance.DEC-01: Whether a screening or unfounded-closure decision must carry any process at all is answered by the Mathews balance, not by any Oklahoma decision.
relevance.DEC-03: The brief's own notes concede that an Oklahoma challenge to a substantiation entry or registry listing must be litigated as a matter of first impression under Mathews and Okla. Const. art. 2, section 7.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the question to the trial court case by case subject to appellate review, and found no error in the failure to appoint counsel on this record.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.FAIL-01: Lassiter is the federal floor against which Oklahoma's broader statutory and state constitutional right to counsel, and the Burrell ineffective-assistance remedy, must be measured.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody, that section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and that section 1915(a) does not bar an adoption when no preferred placement has come forward.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.

relevance.ACT-01: Adoptive Couple is the controlling federal limit on when ICWA requires remedial and rehabilitative services to be offered to a tribal-member parent before rights are severed.
relevance.FAIL-03: It defines when the omission of active efforts is not an ICWA compliance failure at all, and it is the decision Simmers applies in Oklahoma.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to ICWA, holding the Act is within Congress's Article I power over Indian affairs and does not unconstitutionally commandeer the States, and that the petitioners lacked standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation attacks on its placement preferences.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.FAIL-05: Brackeen is the controlling answer to the claim that ICWA's tribal and extended-family placement preferences are race discrimination, and no discrimination analysis of Oklahoma placement practice is complete without it.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session and its majority-opinion text read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization; no ellipses were used and no quote exceeds 30 words.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the OK node files are keyword-match noise. Across all 43 OK files the recurring titles are bar-admission, reinstatement, court-reporter certification, initiative-petition and uniform-jury-instruction adoption orders (e.g. 'IN RE: Rules of the Supreme Court for Mandatory Continuing Legal Education', 'IN RE AMENDMENTS TO RULE 5 ... CERTIFIED SHORTHAND REPORTERS'). None is on point and none was retained. A handful of plausible-looking titles (In re Guardianship of K.D.B., In re Adoption of N.J.B., In re Guardianship of G.E.M.S., In re Guardianship of L.A.C., In re Adoption of A.J.B., In re Adoption of L.B.L.) are recent listings with synthetic citations; searches for the underlying doctrines surfaced better, published authority, so they were not used.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Every Oklahoma Court of Civil Appeals opinion cited carries an official 'OK CIV APP' number, meaning it was released for publication by order of the Court of Civil Appeals or the Supreme Court. Lawyers should still note that under Okla. Sup. Ct. R. 1.200, a released-for-publication COCA opinion has persuasive, not binding, effect unless the Supreme Court has approved it; the Supreme Court decisions listed (In re C.G., A.E., M.R.S., Myers, Ovalle, B.T.W., Daniels, OPEA, West, Vandelay, T.T.S., B.K., M.A.S., In re C.M., S.A.H.) are controlling.

Oklahoma is in the Tenth Circuit. Roska v. Peterson (Utah), Gomes v. Wood (Utah) and T.D. v. Patton (Colorado) are binding circuit law in Oklahoma; Halley v. Huckaby arises directly from Oklahoma DHS and the Eastern District of Oklahoma, and is the most jurisdiction-specific § 1983 child-seizure authority available.

GAPS - nodes with no on-point published Oklahoma appellate authority found, where the federal or state-analogue standard is supplied instead: OUT-04 (extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 under the Chafee Act and Fostering Connections). No Oklahoma published opinion construing 10A O.S. § 1-9-107 or successor extended-jurisdiction provisions was located; the cases mapped (B.T.W. 2008, B.T.W. 2010, K.G., Deal) govern the court's continuing supervision of placement and long-term out-of-home permanency, not the age-21 program itself.

GAPS - DEC-06 (differential / alternative response): no Oklahoma published opinion construes a non-investigation alternative-response track. The cases mapped (M.R.S., Ovalle, In re C.M.) supply the nearest doctrine - the limits of resolving safety concerns outside a court petition and the statutory preference for family preservation - and should be read as analogues, not holdings on DR.

GAPS - substantiated-finding appeal rights and the central registry: no published Oklahoma appellate decision was found addressing a parent's due-process right to an administrative hearing to contest a substantiation entry or a registry listing. DEC-03 is therefore built on the standard-of-proof and notice line (In re C.G., Daniels, Gordon, Frazier) plus the federal floor in Santosky and, now, the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test itself. This is a real hole in Oklahoma law and practitioners should expect to litigate it as a matter of first impression under Okla. Const. art. 2, § 7 and Mathews.

GAPS - records confidentiality and disclosure in child-welfare cases: targeted searches of okla and oklacivapp for DHS record confidentiality returned nothing on point. Oklahoma deprived-case records are confidential by statute (10A O.S. § 1-6-101 et seq.), and no published opinion construing those sections surfaced. FAIL-06 and PMC-05 are therefore built on the general Open Records Act line (OPEA, Vandelay) plus West v. Jane Phillips for confidentiality of reporter-supplied medical information. Expect to argue from the Open Records Act's own child-welfare exemptions rather than from case law.

GAPS - PMC-01 through PMC-06 and INP-09: there is no Oklahoma or Tenth Circuit case law on CFSR monitoring, Single Audit Act or OIG findings, CAPTA § 5106a(c) Citizen Review Panels, or the Protect Our Kids Act fatality commission. CAPTA and the CFSR are widely held to create no privately enforceable right. The cases mapped to these nodes are the closest available Oklahoma authority on public access to agency records (OPEA, Vandelay), agency accountability for a fatal placement (Deal, Bosh, Barrios, T.D. v. Patton, DeShaney) and judicially reviewed reasonable-efforts findings (In re C.M., T.T.S.). They should be presented to readers as adjacent authority, not as decisions about federal oversight mechanisms.

GAPS - FAIL-05 (discrimination / retaliation): a targeted search for race- or religion-based placement discrimination in Oklahoma state courts returned no results. The node is built on ICWA preference litigation (Porter, Cherokee Nation v. L.S., Holyfield, Baby Boy L., Brackeen) and disability-adjacent termination grounds (In re B.K.). No Oklahoma case on MEPA/IEAP, ADA defenses in termination, or retaliation against a reporting parent was located.
GAPS - missing children from foster care: no published Oklahoma appellate decision on absconding, runaway or missing youth in DHS custody was found in CourtListener.

ICWA is unusually central in Oklahoma. Both the federal ICWA and the Oklahoma Indian Child Welfare Act (10 O.S. §§ 40-40.9) apply, and OICWA § 40.6 extends the 25 U.S.C. § 1915 placement preferences to all pre-adjudicatory placements as well as preadoptive, adoptive and foster care placements - broader than the federal text. Practitioners should now read Baby Boy L., M.H.C., Porter, C.H.S., Givens, Smith, Simmers and Clark together, against the federal backdrop of Holyfield, Adoptive Couple and Brackeen.

In re C.G. (1981) remains the leading Oklahoma authority on two distinct points: (1) due process requires judicially prescribed, written norms of parental conduct before a failure-to-correct termination, and (2) the clear-and-convincing standard for termination. Its clear-and-convincing holding is now codified at 10A O.S. § 1-4-904, but C.G. is still the cited source. In re T.T.S. (2015) is the modern procedural counterpart, requiring the specific uncorrected conditions to appear in the application, instructions, verdict forms and final order - a point on which Court of Civil Appeals panels had openly split.

Reporter-immunity practice in Oklahoma is governed by Myers v. Lashley (Okla. 2002): the 10A O.S. § 1-2-104 privilege bars all theories of recovery for reporting-caused harm, good faith is statutorily presumed, and only scienter-level bad faith pierces it. Kremeier (threatened rather than ongoing abuse still immunized; gross negligence insufficient) and West v. Jane Phillips (immunity covers post-reporting harm only, not independently negligent conduct upstream of the report) are the two published COCA refinements.

State v. Gurley is important and cuts against parents: the Court of Civil Appeals held that holding the emergency custody hearing on the third judicial day violated 10A O.S. § 1-4-203's two-judicial-day rule but that the statute supplies no remedy and the court retains jurisdiction, and that the State may re-remove on identical facts after a case is dismissed for missing the seven-day petition deadline. Counsel relying on statutory deadlines in Oklahoma emergency-custody practice should plan around this.

Deal v. Brooks is the key Oklahoma decision on agency liability after a child's death: 51 O.S. § 155(29) exempts DHS from all GTCA tort liability for 'any claim based upon an act or omission of an employee in the placement of children,' but the Court of Civil Appeals held that exemption does not extinguish a Bosh-type damages action directly under the Oklahoma Constitution where DHS employees acted in reckless disregard of a known or obvious risk of serious harm. Both Bosh and Barrios are now carried in the brief, and Barrios must be read before relying on Deal. Compare the federal route in T.D. v. Patton.

API usage: roughly 100 CourtListener requests were made in the original pass and approximately 55 more in this gap-closing pass (about 17 searches, 18 opinion fetches, 20 cluster fetches), paced at one request per 2.2 seconds. No 429 responses were encountered.

Text-quality caveat for citation checkers: several CourtListener plain-text opinions for Oklahoma are OCR conversions containing artifacts (e.g. '0.8.' for 'O.S.', 'clear-and-eonvinc-ing', embedded star-page markers such as '*748'). Quotes were selected to avoid every such artifact, which occasionally meant choosing a slightly narrower sentence than the fullest statement of the rule - most notably in Santosky, where the star-page marker falls inside the Court's central sentence, so the quote begins at 'due process requires' and the surrounding condition ('Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child') is carried in the holding field instead.

Added In the Matter of Baby Boy L., 2004 OK 93, 103 P.3d 1099 (cluster 2632644) for ACT-01, FAIL-03, FAIL-05: the Oklahoma Supreme Court abandoned the judicially created 'existing Indian family' exception and expressly overruled In re S.C., Baby Boy D and D.M.J.; Simmers cannot be cited safely without it, and it is the single most serious omission the verifier identified.

Added In the Matter of A.M. and R.W., 2000 OK 82, 13 P.3d 484 (cluster 2585339) for OUT-02: the Oklahoma Supreme Court's de novo standard of review for procedural due process claims in termination proceedings, and its rule limiting when a parent may be excluded from the courtroom during a child's testimony.

Added Bosh v. Cherokee County Building Authority, 2013 OK 9, 305 P.3d 994 (cluster 5328543) for FAIL-04, OUT-06, PMC-02: the source of the private damages action directly under the Oklahoma Constitution notwithstanding the GTCA, on which Deal v. Brooks is wholly derivative.

Added Barrios v. Haskell County Public Facilities Authority, 2018 OK 90, 432 P.3d 233 (cluster 6657866) for FAIL-04, OUT-06, PMC-02: the Supreme Court's later, narrowing treatment of Bosh, holding the 2014 GTCA amendments made 'constitutional torts' torts governed by the Act - decided after Deal and essential to assessing whether the Deal route to liability survives.

Added In the Matter of M.H.C., 2016 OK 88 (cluster 4258132) for INP-11: the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court decision on ICWA transfer and 'good cause,' expressly relied on in the brief's own C.H.S. opinion; INP-11 previously rested on Court of Civil Appeals decisions alone for the transfer burden.

Added Matter of Chad S., 1978 OK 94, 580 P.2d 983 (cluster 1193572) for FAIL-01: the foundational Oklahoma due-process authority in child deprivation cases, the source of the 'full panoply of procedural safeguards' language quoted from T.T.S., and the decision requiring that an indigent parent be advised of the right to appointed counsel.

Added In the Matter of J.D.H., 2006 OK 5, 130 P.3d 245 (cluster 2622689) for DEC-02, DEC-05, INP-10: the Supreme Court's statement of the competent-evidence standard for reviewing a deprived adjudication, relied on in Gurley, plus its treatment of a therapist relaying a child's statements.

Added Michael F. v. State ex rel. Department of Human Services (In the Matter of D.D.F.), 1990 OK 89, 801 P.2d 703 (cluster 5332639) for FAIL-01: the Oklahoma Supreme Court holding that the right to counsel in a termination proceeding includes effective assistance measured by an objective standard of reasonableness - the premise Burrell builds its ineffective-assistance procedure on.

Added Muggenborg v. Kessler, 1981 OK 66, 630 P.2d 1276 (cluster 1167062) for ACT-04, OUT-03: the Supreme Court holding that a grandparent with a co-equal custodial claim has standing and is constitutionally entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard; it is the authority Katherine E. applies.

Added In re Adoption of K.P.M.A., 2014 OK 85, 341 P.3d 38 (cluster 2742197) for OUT-02: the controlling Supreme Court decision on the notice a biological father is owed before his consent right may be severed, relied on in M.A.S.

Added In the Matter of the Adoption of R.W.S., 1997 OK 148, 951 P.2d 83 (cluster 2611413) for OUT-02: the Supreme Court's statement that eligibility for adoption without parental consent must be proved by clear and convincing evidence and that nonsupport must be willful; also relied on in M.A.S. and Baby Boy L.

Added In the Matter of B.T.W., 2010 OK 69, 241 P.3d 199 (cluster 2380270) for OUT-01, ACT-03, OUT-04: the SECOND, later Oklahoma Supreme Court B.T.W. decision, cited in In re C.M. for the reasonable-efforts abuse-of-discretion standard. It must be distinguished by year from 2008 OK 80, 195 P.3d 896, which the brief already carried; the two are separate appeals in the same case and both are now listed with distinct cluster ids (2636500 for 2008, 2380270 for 2010).

Department of Social Services of Durham County, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) (cluster 110506) for FAIL-01: the federal baseline on appointed counsel in termination proceedings, the necessary companion to Chad S., D.D.F. and Burrell. Added Oklahoma Public Employees Ass'n v. State ex rel. Oklahoma Office of Personnel Management, 2011 OK 68, 267 P.3d 838 (cluster 5326712) for FAIL-06, PMC-02, PMC-03, PMC-05: the brief's prior notes cited 'OPEA' repeatedly as the general Open Records Act authority without carrying it as an entry. Missing (for a later pass): In re S.B.C., 2002 OK 83, 64 P.3d 1080 — the Oklahoma Supreme Court's standard for appellate review of a termination judgment for clear and convincing evidence; relied on by K.P.M.A. (now in the brief) and by Daniels, yet OUT-02 and FAIL-01 carry no entry for the review standard itself.

Missing (for a later pass): In re T.R.W., 1985 OK 99, 722 P.2d 1197 — the source of the competent-evidence standard for reviewing a deprived adjudication that In re J.D.H. quotes for the very proposition the brief's J.D.H. quote states; DEC-05 rests on the derivative case without carrying the original.

Missing (for a later pass): In re J.B., 1982 OK 40, 643 P.2d 306 — the Oklahoma Supreme Court decision fixing the preponderance burden at the deprived-adjudication stage, cited in J.D.H. alongside the statute; DEC-05 and DEC-03 both turn on the preponderance versus clear-and-convincing distinction and should cite it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.S., 2010 OK 46, 237 P.3d 161 — the decision M.H.C. relies on for the rule that the party opposing ICWA transfer must prove good cause by clear and convincing evidence; INP-11 carries M.H.C. and C.H.S. but not the authority they both apply.

Missing (for a later pass): Steltzlen v. Fritz, 2006 OK 20, 134 P.3d 141 — states the clear-and-convincing standard and the burden on a party seeking adoption without parental consent, and is the authority K.P.M.A. cites for it; OUT-02 is built on that line without it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Baby Boy W., 1999 OK 74, 988 P.2d 1270 — the foundational Oklahoma holding on an unwed father's constitutionally protected opportunity interest and right to notice of the pregnancy; K.P.M.A. is decided expressly 'pursuant to this Court's decision in Baby Boy W. and its progeny,' so OUT-02 cites the progeny without the parent case.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Darren Todd H., 1980 OK 119, 615 P.2d 287 — the original Oklahoma statement that eligibility for adoption without parental consent must be proved by clear and convincing evidence and that willfulness is a fact question; quoted as the source in both R.W.S. and K.P.M.A.

Missing (for a later pass): Vanderpool v. State, 1983 OK 82, 672 P.2d 1153 — abolished common-law sovereign immunity in Oklahoma and is the decision Barrios invokes when describing the Legislature's power to define the State's immunity; FAIL-04 and OUT-06 turn entirely on the Bosh/Barrios immunity arc and are incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Rich, 1979 OK 173, 604 P.2d 1248 — holds an incarcerated parent is entitled to a fair and meaningful opportunity to defend in a family-status suit though physical presence is not the only means; it is the authority A.M. and R.W. builds on and the natural companion to the brief's incarcerated-parent entries (Khan, H.M.W., T.T.S.).
